title: African theology
hookLine: John Mbiti: I am because we are, and the Christian God was already sought in Africa

lines: A STUDENT COMES HOME TO KENYA.
A PERSON IS A THREAD IN A CLOTH.
cards: Ask who you are, and you'll probably give a name, a job, a town. Now ask it another way: who are you with? John Mbiti grew up in Kenya hearing that question answered the second way.
He went abroad to study theology, read the great European books, and came home with a puzzle. Many of those books, as he saw it, started with the lonely individual: I think, I choose, I believe.
The villages he knew started with family, with neighbors, with the ancestors and the children not yet born. A person was a thread in a cloth.
Mbiti spent his life asking what the gospel sounds like when you start from the cloth.

teach.b: Mbiti, an Anglican priest and scholar, is one of the voices people mean by African theology. First, his summary of how, as he saw it, many African peoples understand a person: I am, because we are.
The community makes the person. It flips the well-known European line about thinking and existing. You aren't first a self who then joins a group; you become a self through the people who hold you.
Second, the Bible's own picture of that shape.

teach.h: ONE BODY: SHARED PAIN, SHARED JOY.
teach.b: Paul calls the church a body: "whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it."

In Acts, the first believers "continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." The Greek word behind fellowship, koinonia, means sharing in common.

Third, God was not a stranger. Mbiti gathered the ways African peoples had long spoken of God: creator, provider, the one who sees. He argued that missionaries didn't carry God into Africa as if God had been absent.

The gospel came as an answer to a search already under way. Paul says something close in Athens: God made the nations so "that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him."
A faith that starts from we notices who's missing from the table.

how: In African churches, as elsewhere, Christians pray for their families, neighbors and those who came before them by name, and gather to share both mourning and celebration as a community.

games.q: you're John Mbiti, home from studying abroad. the books you read start from the lonely I. your village starts from we. what do you do?
o: drop the village's way of seeing; the books are the real theology.
start from the we, and read the Bible again from there.
games.why: Mbiti started from the community, and argued that the gospel came to people already seeking God. read beside him, scripture has its own picture: one body, fellowship.

practice: Let the people who made you come to mind one at a time, a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor who fed you, a friend from a hard year, and to each say quietly: because you were, I am.
If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if not, notice how many hands are in your story. Then, if you like, think of someone for whom you are one of those hands.

wordCard.voice: African theology. In John Mbiti's hands, faith that starts from the we, and a God who was already being sought before any missionary arrived.

orig.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing in common. the word in Acts 2:42 for the first believers' life together.

carryVoice: Your line: I am because we are. Nobody becomes a self alone. Same time tomorrow.
